questions.q: What are the three ingredients that define a combinatorial optimization problem?
options: Decision variables, an objective function, and constraints
A continuous curve, a derivative, and a learning rate
A quantum circuit, a Hamiltonian, and a measurement
A training set, a loss function, and a neural network
questions.explain: Every combinatorial optimization problem is defined by discrete decision variables to choose, an objective function scoring any choice, and constraints that rule out invalid combinations.

questions.q: With n binary decision variables, how many candidate solutions exist in the full search space?
options: 2n
n!
questions.explain: Each of the n binary variables can independently be 0 or 1, so the total number of combinations is 2^n -- which grows explosively even for modest n.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say a finite number of choices does NOT mean the problem is easy?
options: Because the number of candidate solutions grows combinatorially (2^n) with the number of variables, quickly exceeding what brute force can search
Because finite problems always require continuous calculus to solve
Because finite search spaces cannot be represented on a computer
Because combinatorial problems have no objective function
questions.explain: 2^n grows so fast that even moderate n (a few hundred variables) produces a search space larger than the number of atoms in the observable universe, making brute force impossible regardless of hardware speed.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the three business-shaped examples given in the lesson?
options: Training a deep neural network on labeled images
Portfolio selection (choosing a subset of assets)
Vehicle routing (the Traveling Salesman Problem)
Shift scheduling for workers
questions.explain: The lesson's three examples are portfolio selection, vehicle routing/TSP, and shift scheduling -- all discrete combinatorial problems. Neural network training is a continuous optimization problem solved by gradient descent, not the combinatorial shape this course targets.

questions.q: According to the lesson, what is the honest relationship between NP-hard combinatorial problems and quantum optimization algorithms like QAOA?
options: QAOA and quantum annealers are heuristics too -- they search for good solutions without guaranteeing the provably best one, the same way classical heuristics do
QAOA provably solves all NP-hard problems in polynomial time, unlike any classical method
NP-hard problems become easy once translated into a QUBO
Quantum computers can brute-force 2^n search spaces instantly regardless of n
questions.explain: The lesson is explicit that quantum optimization methods are heuristics in the same sense as simulated annealing or genetic algorithms -- they look for good answers efficiently, not a proven optimum, and this course avoids overselling that distinction.
